clinicalPearls: Classically affects women of childbearing age who are overweight, with recent weight gain a common precipitant
Typical symptoms are headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus and horizontal diplopia from a sixth nerve palsy (a false localising sign of raised pressure)
The cardinal sign is bilateral papilloedema, which distinguishes true disc swelling from pseudopapilloedema such as disc drusen

Diagnosis follows modified Dandy criteria: signs of raised intracranial pressure, normal neuroimaging (with no mass, hydrocephalus or venous thrombosis), and a raised opening pressure on lumbar puncture with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition
Visual field testing typically shows an enlarged blind spot and progressive nerve fibre bundle defects, and is central to monitoring
Optical coherence tomography quantifies peripapillary nerve fibre layer swelling and helps track response to treatment
Management principles combine weight loss with carbonic anhydrase inhibition (acetazolamide) to reduce cerebrospinal fluid production, reserving surgery for sight-threatening disease
Fulminant IIH with rapid visual loss requires urgent intervention such as optic nerve sheath fenestration or cerebrospinal fluid diversion
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a disorder of raised intracranial pressure in the absence of a mass lesion, hydrocephalus, infection or venous sinus thrombosis. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve impaired cerebrospinal fluid absorption and possibly increased production, together with cerebral venous and metabolic factors linked to obesity. The elevated pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths, obstructing axoplasmic flow at the optic disc and producing papilloedema. Persistent disc swelling leads to progressive optic nerve fibre loss and irreversible visual field constriction if the pressure is not controlled.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant hypertension with hypertensive disc oedema
Optic disc drusen and other causes of pseudopapilloedema
Bilateral optic neuritis or infiltrative optic neuropathy
Medication-induced intracranial hypertension (for example tetracyclines, retinoids, excess vitamin A)
additionalInvestigations: Neuroimaging, preferably MRI with venography, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure and confirm normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents
Automated perimetry to detect and monitor blind spot enlargement and field loss
Optical coherence tomography of the peripapillary nerve fibre layer to grade and follow disc swelling
Dilated fundus examination and disc photography to document papilloedema severity
Blood pressure measurement and review of medications and recent weight change
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual field loss or reduced acuity indicating fulminant disease
Severe papilloedema with haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots or macular involvement
New focal neurological deficit beyond a sixth nerve palsy, suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Imaging evidence of venous sinus thrombosis or a mass requiring specific treatment
reference.prognosis: With weight loss and medical therapy, most patients have a good visual outcome, but a subset, particularly those with fulminant disease or poor adherence, suffer permanent optic atrophy and visual field loss; the condition can be chronic and relapsing and headaches may persist despite controlled pressure.
pitfalls: Labelling the condition idiopathic without excluding venous sinus thrombosis and secondary causes
Mistaking pseudopapilloedema from disc drusen for true papilloedema and over-investigating, or the reverse
Relying on symptoms and treating headache while missing silent progressive visual field loss
Overlooking a causative medication such as tetracyclines or retinoids
Delaying surgical intervention in fulminant disease until vision is irretrievably lost
management: Achieve weight loss as the key disease-modifying intervention, with dietary support and consideration of bariatric surgery in appropriate patients
Lower intracranial pressure medically with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide), using topiramate or a diuretic as alternatives
Review and withdraw precipitating agents such as tetracyclines, retinoids and excess vitamin A
Monitor vision closely with serial automated perimetry, optic disc assessment and optical coherence tomography, as sight loss is the major morbidity
For fulminant or treatment-resistant disease with threatened vision, escalate to surgery such as optic nerve sheath fenestration, cerebrospinal fluid diversion or venous sinus stenting
Manage headache symptomatically and use therapeutic lumbar puncture as a temporising measure
Coordinate care within a multidisciplinary team of ophthalmology, neurology and neurosurgery
